## Observed Facts

- **Teams cannot be determined from these logs.** The BGL dataset exposes only `alert_tag`, `component`, `level`, and `node` as columns, with no owner or team field [E2]. Team ownership has to come from a separate source.
- **FATAL Log Entries by BGL Component** (Data Scope: BGL, full corpus 2005-06-03 to 2006-01-04, level = FATAL, no other filters) [E1]:
  - KERNEL: 626,450 Log Entries (about 73%)
  - APP: 228,536 Log Entries (about 27%)
  - LINKCARD: 206 Log Entries
  - MMCS: 3 Log Entries
  - Total: 855,195 Log Entries across 4 Components [E1]
- KERNEL and APP together account for essentially all FATAL Log Entries. LINKCARD and MMCS are negligible by comparison.
- These are Log Entry counts, not incidents. A single failure can produce many entries.

## Hypotheses

- Ownership for KERNEL and APP would matter most, since they carry nearly all FATAL volume. This is an inference from the counts, not something the logs confirm.

## Unknowns

- Which Team owns each Component. Nothing in the log data identifies Teams, so the mapping must come from your ownership records or service catalog.
- Whether the FATAL volume is spread across many incidents or concentrated in a few recurring faults. I have not checked this. A trend or a per-`alert_tag` breakdown would show it.
- Whether the same volume pattern holds for the time period you care about. The counts above cover the full corpus only.

## Next Step

1. Get the Component-to-Team mapping for KERNEL, APP, LINKCARD, and MMCS from your ownership source.
2. Then I can run a per-`alert_tag` breakdown for KERNEL and APP and a trend over time, so you can see whether the FATAL volume recurs or comes from a few spikes. Tell me if you want a specific date range.
